title.en: Marie Laveau: the Last Voodoo Queen
title.zh: 瑪麗·拉沃：末代伏都女王

region.zh: 美國路易斯安那紐奧良

texts.period: Louisiana Voodoo; queen flourished 1820s-1880s; recorded 1920s; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III 'Voodooism and Conjuration' — section 'Marie Laveau'

summary.en: New Orleans's last voodoo queen, half legend half history: at her funeral the superstitious crowds expected supernatural occurrences, and said the live snake she had fed under her bed like a baby was the devil come to claim her soul. An old Frenchman who knew her called the legends pure fancy — a hair-dresser and procuress afraid of snakes, who kept a small jointed wooden snake on the mantel to fool the superstitious — so great a web of fancy has been woven around this unique character that a painting of her unsellable at two dollars after her death is now worth over two hundred and fifty.
summary.zh: 紐奧良末代伏都女王，傳說與史實各半：她的葬禮上迷信的民眾專候異象，說她如嬰兒般在床下飼養的活蛇，是來索她靈魂的魔鬼。一位相識的老法國人卻稱傳說純屬虛構——她不過是髮妝師兼拉皮條者，怕蛇，只把一條小木蛇擺在壁爐架上愚弄迷信者——圍繞這位奇女子的傳說之網織得如此之厚，她死後兩美元賣不出的畫像，如今值二百五十美元。

sensitivity.note: Historical-folkloric portrait of a named New Orleans figure from Puckett's 1920s fieldwork; conflicting testimonies preserved (snake story vs. wooden-snake story). Living-tradition figures treated with care; no ritual reproduction.

passages.text: Marie Laveau was the last voodoo queen, and in Puckett's investigation of voodooism in New Orleans he found many conflicting views regarding her. A member of the Historical Society distinctly remembers her funeral, which was attended by large numbers of superstitious Negroes, all expecting supernatural occurrences.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro, ch. III, section 'Marie Laveau' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of those Negroes stated that Marie Laveau had a live snake which she kept under her bed and fed like a baby; when its mistress died the snake departed, and the Negroes said it was the devil gone to claim her soul. An old Frenchman, a personal friend of Marie Laveau, stated that a great deal at present said about her is pure fancy and fiction: she was simply a griffe — the offspring of a Negro and a mulattress — a procuress and a hair-dresser, visiting the homes of her clients and using her intimate knowledge gathered there in dealing with related white customers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: As a matter of fact, Marie Laveau, so he states from personal knowledge of her house, was afraid of snakes, but kept a small jointed wooden snake on her mantel along with other bric-a-brac to fool the superstitious. So great has been the web of fancy woven around this unique character that an original painting of her, which an antique dealer could not sell for two dollars just after her death, is now worth over two hundred and fifty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Voodoo Dance and the Monter-Voudou

region.zh: 美國路易斯安那紐奧良

texts.period: Louisiana Voodoo (19th-c. societies described via Castellanos); recorded 1920s; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III, section 'Louisiana Voodoo Rites' (synthesizing Castellanos and Cable)

summary.en: The night ceremony of the voodoo society: red handkerchiefs at the loins, the king with his blue cord and crimson drape, adoration of the snake in its barred cage on the altar and renewal of the oath of secrecy; the queen set bodily upon the box of the deity, seized with convulsions while the oracle talks through her inspired lips; the candidate in the charcoal circle with his package of herbs and waxen effigies, the paddle-tap, the African chant — 'Eh! eh! Bomba, hen, hen! Canga bafio te...' — and the squirming dance called monter-voudou, until pandemonium is let loose.
summary.zh: 伏都社的夜祭：腰繫紅帕、頭纏紅布的王，祭壇柵籠中的蛇受眾膜拜，守密之誓重申；王后被親手放上神匣，痙攣之中神諭借她之口說話；候補者立於炭圈，手捧藥草與蠟像之包，木槳輕擊，非洲古調起——『嗡！嗡！邦巴，喝！喝！康加巴菲奧……』——扭動之舞名為『上伏都』，直至群魔亂舞。

sensitivity.note: Historical reconstruction of 19th-century Louisiana Voodoo rites from published sources (Castellanos, Cable) synthesized by Puckett; the chant is transcribed as folklore in those sources. Living-tradition practice is not reproduced beyond the public-domain description; the same ceremony is documented from the hostile St. John account (cross_ref: vodou-serpent-ceremony).

passages.text: The secret meetings of the voodoo society were held at night. Castellanos tells of the members divesting themselves of their usual raiment and putting on sandals, girding their loins with red handkerchiefs — of which the king wears a greater number and those of finer quality than the ordinary member; he also has a blue cord about his waist and his head draped with some crimson stuff, while the queen is dressed more simply, with red garments and a red sash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro, ch. III, 'Louisiana Voodoo Rites' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ceremony begins with the adoration of the snake, placed in a barred cage upon an altar in front of the king and queen, and a renewal of the oath of secrecy. The king and queen extol future happiness and exhort their subjects always to seek their advice; then individually the members come up to implore the voodoo god — to invoke blessings upon friends and curses upon enemies. The king patiently listens. Then the spirit moves him: he places the queen bodily upon the box containing the deity. She is seized with convulsions and the oracle talks through her inspired lips — bestowing flattery and promises of success, then laying down irrevocable laws in the name of the serpent. Questions are asked and an offering taken; new work is proposed and the oath of secrecy again taken, sometimes sealed by the warm blood of a kid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: After this the voodoo dance begins. The initiation of new candidates forms the first part of the ceremony: the voodoo king traces a large circle in the center of the room with a piece of charcoal and places within it the sable neophyte, thrusting into his hand a package of herbs, horse hair, rancid tallow, waxen effigies, broken bits of horn, and other substances. Then, lightly striking him on the head with a small wooden paddle, he launches into the African chant — 'Eh! eh! Bomba, hen, hen! Canga bafio te, Canga moune de le, Canga do ki la, Canga li' — and at this the candidate begins to squirm and dance, an action called monter-voudou; if he steps out of the ring in his frenzy the king and queen turn their backs to neutralize the bad omen. Drinking some stimulant, he relapses into a hysterical fit; the initiate is then led to the altar to take the oath, and from that moment becomes a full-fledged member of the order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king then places his foot upon the box containing the snake; he seems to get a sort of shock which is transmitted to his queen, and through her to everyone in the circle. Violent convulsions take place, the queen being the most violently affected; from time to time the serpent is again touched to get more magnetic power. The box is shaken, and the tinkling bells on its side increase the general delirium already under way, aggravated by much drinking of spirituous liquors — 'then is pandemonium let loose': fainting fits and choking spells succeed one another, a nervous tremor possesses everybody, they spin with incredible velocity, and some, entirely deprived of reason, fall down to the ground from sheer lassitude and are carried still panting and gyrating.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Self-made Hoodoo-doctor: Fieldwork Among the Trick-doctors
title.zh: 自封的呼督醫：深入巫醫圈的田野調查

region.en: Mississippi and Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國密西西比與喬治亞種植園地帶

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III, sections 'A Self-made Hoodoo-doctor', 'Professional Duties', 'Satisfied Patients'

summary.en: The ethnographer turns conjure-doctor to hoodoo the hoodoos: a startling collection of red flannel rags, rabbit's feet, lodestone and steel filings, an Egyptian idol, a jack, graveyard dirt, voodoo charms from New Orleans — and patients come. Professional duties follow: diagnose who laid the trick, find and destroy the charm, turn the trick back, lay haunts, locate treasure and water. The satisfied patients include an old woman cured — 'strange to say' — of sickness by a doctor's self-buried bottle of hair and graveyard dirt, and a man who died still believing in the lizards the conjurer had slipped into his poultice.
summary.zh: 民族誌者自任巫醫，以呼督制呼督：一袋紅法蘭絨、兔腳、磁石鋼屑、埃及偶像、墓土與紐奧良符物——患者自來。其職司包括診斷誰施咒、尋咒毀咒、以咒還咒、置鬼尋寶找水。『滿意』的病人中：一位老嫗被巫醫自埋的『頭髮墓土』咒瓶診出、破解——『說來奇怪』竟痊癒；另一人至死仍信臂中有蜥蜴——蜥蜴是巫醫親手塞進藥泥的。

sensitivity.note: Puckett's participant-observation among 1920s conjure-doctors, including named cases (Steiner's Georgia cases cited). Recorded as ethnographic narrative of folk practice; no working instructions beyond what the source records as anecdote. Living-tradition caution: conjure practice is part of a living religion; material presented historically.

passages.text: In almost all cases the conjure-doctor is a peculiar individual, set aside because of his very peculiarity for dealings with the supernatural; not always are the conjure-doctors Negroes — sometimes white women assume the role for the sake of the rewards to be gained by successful imposture. After being asked to pay twenty dollars for some trifling information by Negroes he had good reason to believe were hoodoos, Puckett finally adopted the role of conjure-doctor himself, in order to be able to discuss the tricks of the trade as hoodoo to hoodoo: 'Even conjurers are not without their professional spirit, and I found them quite willing to swap clinical knowledge and even materia medica with one, once they believed him to be a real trick-doctor.' His startling collection of red flannel rags, rabbit's feet, lodestone and steel filings, an Egyptian idol, a jack, graveyard dirt, voodoo charms from New Orleans — and enough imagination to conjure up missing details when necessary — soon had patients seeking his aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'A Self-made Hoodoo-doctor' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Professional duties: one of the first things the conjure-doctors have to do is to diagnose the case, tell the person whether he is conjured or not, and find out who laid the trick; the trick — the charm — must be found and destroyed and the patient cured; if the patient wishes, the conjurer must also be able to turn the trick back upon the one who set it. Besides this, a conjurer truly up in his profession must be able to lay haunts, and to locate buried treasure or a vein of water: treasure by a divining rod with a nail in the end of each branching twig, marching boldly over the suspected landscape — when you pass over the buried treasure the free end will be pulled suddenly toward the ground — or water by observing a tree whose limbs are longer on one side, bending in that direction where the vein lies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'Professional Duties' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Satisfied patients: Puckett tested this out on his own clients — a quarter down, let the client keep the charm a week, two dollars more if satisfied; in very few cases was the client unwilling to pay. True there is often trickery: in one case an old Negro woman was taken sick, and a scheming conjure-doctor at once buried a bottle containing human hair, graveyard dirt and two small sticks in the path leading to her spring, told her she was conjured, offered to find the conjure for ten dollars; roaming over the location with a little iron rod, he located the charm he had buried, broke the bottle and buried it in the middle of the public road, and gave the old woman some roots to chew. She gladly paid the ten dollars and, strange to say, recovered — illustrating the power of mind over body; although the trick was exposed she still believes that she was conjured and that she was cured by the doctor. In another case, a man had a rising on his arm; the conjure-doctor slipped a lizard into a poultice which he bound on the sore, and later, taking the poultice off, told the man he was conjured and had lizards in his arm — and although the hoodoo-doctor collected considerable money in an attempt to cure the trouble, the patient finally died, thinking to the last that he had reptiles in his arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'Satisfied Patients' (1926); not verbatim.

region.en: Deep South crossroads, USA (symbolic pin: Mississippi Delta)
region.zh: 美國深南部十字路口（象徵定位：密西西比三角洲）

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II 'Burial Customs, Ghosts, and Witches' — section 'The Origin of Jack' (told by a root-doctor)

summary.en: The wandering flame of the swamps has a biography: Jack sold himself to the devil at the crossroads one night at twelve o'clock; for seven years all power was given him to do as he pleased, but at the end of that period his soul belonged to the devil — until Jack, ready, tacked a piece of old shoe sole above the door, asked the devil to fetch it, nailed the reaching hand fast and slipped the chair away, and was freed on his promise — whereupon neither heaven nor hell would have him, and he wanders with his lantern still.
summary.zh: 沼澤間的游火有著自己的傳記：傑克於午夜十二時在十字路口將自己賣給魔鬼；七年之內百般自在，期滿靈魂便歸魔鬼——然而傑克早有準備：門楣上釘了一塊舊鞋底，請魔鬼代取；魔鬼立椅伸手之際，傑克掄錘釘住其手、抽走椅凳，換得釋放之諾——此後天堂地獄皆不收他，他便提著燈籠永世游蕩。

sensitivity.note: Jack-o'-lantern origin legend told to Puckett by a root-doctor; the turn-the-pocket-out defense recorded alongside (cross-ref: harris Spirits tale; owen Wuller-wups).

passages.text: The Southern Negroes are very familiar with the apparition which they call Jack-o'-lantern, or Jack-o'-my-lantern, though the whites of the locality pay little or no attention to such beliefs — making this a bit of English lore preserved almost exclusively by Negroes. These Jack-o'-lanterns carry lights and would certainly fool you into the swamp or river, unless you turn your pockets wrongside out — doubtless to show the avaricious spirit that you have nothing in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'Jack-o'-my-Lantern' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Various legends are in vogue among the Negroes to account for the origin of this creature. One illustrating the common theme was told Puckett by a root-doctor: Jack sold himself to the devil at the crossroads one night at twelve o'clock. For seven years all power was given to him to do as he pleased, but at the end of that period his soul belonged to the devil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'The Origin of Jack' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Satan called for him, but Jack was ready. He had tacked a piece of old shoe sole up above the door, and asked the devil to get it for him. The devil stood in a chair and reached for it; Jack then took a hammer and nailed the devil's hand fast, slipping the chair out from under him — and upon a promise of his freedom, the devil went his way, and Jack went his: a soul that hell would not take and heaven would not have, carrying his lantern through the swamps ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Coolin'-Board Wake: Ashes That Take Up the Disease

region.en: Virginia and the Deep South, USA
region.zh: 美國弗吉尼亞與深南部

texts.period: African-American mortuary practice; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II, sections on wakes and the coolin'-board (citing Smiley's Virginia-Carolina-Georgia-Florida folklore)

summary.en: Between death and burial the body is never left alone: neighbors come and set up, food is served and melodies sung — the spontaneous rhythmic grief at these wakes being, in Puckett's judgment, the beginning of many spirituals. On the coolin'-board a plateful of salt and ashes stands beneath the sheets — whatever disease the body has goes into the ashes and salt, 'ashes takes up from the body the disease' — and at the words 'ashes to ashes and dust to dust' they are thrown into the grave; the last one to leave a settin'-up will be the first one to die.
summary.zh: 入土之前，遺體不可片刻無人：鄰里前來守靈，進食歌唱——這種守靈時自發而合拍的悲歌，在普凱特看來正是許多靈歌的源頭。涼板之上、褥單之下置一盤鹽與灰——死者身中何病，皆入灰鹽——『灰自身上吸去其病』；誦到『歸於塵土』之句，便將其傾入墓中；守靈最後離開的人，將是最先死去的人。

sensitivity.note: Mortuary-folklore description from published ethnography (Puckett citing Smiley, JAF 1919); no ritual instruction beyond the description; presented as documentary folk belief.

passages.text: During the three days — sometimes less — elapsing between death and burial, the body should never be left alone. Neighbors come and set up with the body; food is served and melodies sung — the spontaneous expression of grief in rhythmic form at this time probably being the beginning of many spirituals. The older Negroes complain that wakes are not what they used to be: 'We used to sing and pray all the night long, but now the young folks that attend them just tells anecdotes all night.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: In other localities the body is placed on a coolin'-board and covered with an arrangement of sheets, the one over the face being raised when the mourners address the corpse: 'Mandy, you gone and left me... I may be next... Poor Mandy!... Poor John!' A plateful of salt and ashes is placed under the coolin'-board, and whatever disease the body has goes into the ashes and salt — 'Ashes takes up from the body the disease.' These ashes are carried to the grave, and at the words 'Ashes to ashes and dust to dust' they are thrown into the grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926), citing Smiley (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: No one would think of leaving a settin'-up alone, and the last one to leave such a meeting will be the first one to die. This idea of a wake may be either European or African in origin; and the African has an intense passion for burials — even pawning himself and his children into slavery if need be to give his relations a proper funeral — while the Southern Negro has much the same notion, paying dues to a lodge all his life, or going head over heels into debt, to see that he or his relations are laid away in style.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: Feet First: the Funeral Procession Rules
title.zh: 腳朝前：出殯行列的規矩

texts.period: African-American mortuary practice; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II, section 'The Funeral Procession'

summary.en: The corpse is taken from the house feet first, else it would be looking back and beckoning a member of the family to follow; touch the body once and the ghost will not harm you; never carry a corpse in its own vehicle — a hearse should always be hired — and never let it stop between the house and the cemetery, all gates being opened beforehand; if the procession stops, another death will soon follow, for a mishap on the way indicates that the corpse is dissatisfied; and the person who counts the carriages in the procession is only counting the days before his own death.
summary.zh: 遺體抬出家門必須腳朝前，否則亡者會回望招手，引家人隨行；摸過遺體一次，鬼魂便不害你；不可用死者自己的車運屍——靈車必須僱用——從家到墓園途中不得停歇，事先應把所有柵門打開；行列若停，死亡將接踵而至，因途中受阻意味著亡者戀世不捨；而數點送葬馬車的人，數的正是自己餘下的日子。

sensitivity.note: Mortuary omens compiled by Puckett from southern informants; presented as documentary folk belief.

passages.text: When the time comes for burial the corpse should be taken from the house feet first, else it would be looking back and beckoning to a member of the family to follow — a belief European in origin, as is also the common Negro belief that if you put your hand on the corpse the ghost will not harm you (or you will be afraid of no more dead people). This may be the remnant of an old ordeal, since wounds are supposed to bleed if the murderer touches the corpse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'The Funeral Procession' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is extremely bad luck to carry a corpse to the cemetery in his own vehicle — a hearse should always be hired. The corpse should not be allowed to stop between the house and the cemetery (with the exception of the church), all gates being opened beforehand. If the procession should stop, another death will soon follow — a mishap on the way probably indicating that the corpse is dissatisfied and regrets having to leave this world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: A person who counts the carriages in the funeral procession does no more than count the days before his own death — a belief of European origin. While it is extremely bad luck to walk ahead of the corpse, it is even worse luck to meet a funeral procession face to face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, ending (1926); not verbatim.
